text: If the facts don't hang together on a latticework of theory, you don't have them in a usable form.
source: A Lesson on Elementary, Worldly Wisdom
context: Opening rule of his April 14, 1994 talk to Professor Guilford Babcock's students at the USC Business School, later collected in Poor Charlie's Almanack.

text: You've got to have models in your head. And you've got to array your experience — both vicarious and direct — on this latticework of models.
source: A Lesson on Elementary, Worldly Wisdom
context: His case that isolated facts fail in school and in life unless experience is hung on a set of models.

text: The models have to come from multiple disciplines — because all the wisdom of the world is not to be found in one little academic department.
source: A Lesson on Elementary, Worldly Wisdom
context: Why a single specialty, the man-with-a-hammer problem, is a disastrous way to operate.

text: It is given to human beings who work hard at it — who look and sift the world for a mispriced bet — that they can occasionally find one.
source: A Lesson on Elementary, Worldly Wisdom
context: His pari-mutuel model of investing: you will not know everything, but a hard search sometimes turns up a mispriced bet worth loading up on.

text: There are huge advantages for an individual to get into a position where you make a few great investments and just sit back and wait.
source: A Lesson on Elementary, Worldly Wisdom
context: Fewer brokers, less nonsense, and a tax system that rewards long holding periods in great companies.

text: Getting the incentives right is a very, very important lesson.
source: A Lesson on Elementary, Worldly Wisdom
context: The moral of his Federal Express night-shift story: pay by the shift, not the hour, and the sort cleared overnight.

text: The constant curse of scale is that it leads to big, dumb bureaucracy.
source: A Lesson on Elementary, Worldly Wisdom
context: Scale cuts costs, then breeds bureaucracies that think the work is done when a paper leaves the in-basket.

text: The safest way to try to get what you want is to try to deserve what you want.
source: USC Gould School of Law Commencement
context: The first idea in his May 13, 2007 commencement address: deliver what you would buy if you were on the other end.

text: You want to deliver to the world what you would buy if you were on the other end.
source: USC Gould School of Law Commencement
context: His plain statement of the golden rule for lawyers and everyone else.

text: The acquisition of wisdom is a moral duty.
source: USC Gould School of Law Commencement
context: Not a career tactic. The corollary is lifetime learning, because what you already know will not carry you.

text: I constantly see people rise in life who are not the smartest, sometimes not even the most diligent. But they are learning machines. They go to bed every night a little wiser than they were that morning.
source: USC Gould School of Law Commencement
context: The habit he says helps most when you have a long run ahead of you.

text: If you turn problems around into reverse, you often think better.
source: USC Gould School of Law Commencement
context: His own statement of inversion, after retelling the rustic who wanted to know where he would die so he would never go there.

text: I feel that I'm not entitled to have an opinion unless I can state the arguments against my position better than the people who are in opposition.
source: USC Gould School of Law Commencement
context: The rule he uses to keep intense ideology from cabbaging up the only mind he will ever have.

text: Another thing you have to do is have a lot of assiduity. I like that word because to me it means: sit down on your ass until you do it.
source: USC Gould School of Law Commencement
context: His gloss on the unglamorous persistence he credits in the partners he admires.
